ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A small charged ball with mass $\mathbf{m}$ and charge $+q$ (considered as a point mass) is suspended by an inextensible insulating light string at point A directly below point O. A uniform electric field is applied horizontally to the right. The ball is released from rest at point A and reaches the highest point B. It is known that the angle between OA and OB is $\uptheta\!=\!60^{\circ}$, the length of the string is $L$, the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g$, and air resistance is negligible.

1. Find the magnitude of the electric field strength $E$.
2. Determine the magnitude of the tension force $F$ when the speed of the small ball is at its maximum.

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A small charged ball with mass $m$ and charge $+q$ (considered as a point mass) is suspended by an inextensible insulating light string at point A directly below point O. A uniform electric field is applied horizontally to the right. The ball is released from rest at point A and reaches the highest point B. It is known that the angle between OA and OB is $\theta = 60^\circ$, the length of the string is $L$, the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g$, and air resistance is negligible. 1. Find the magnitude of the electric field strength $E$. 2. Determine the magnitude of the tension force $F$ when the speed of the small ball is at its maximum.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the fixed point above is labeled O, and a thin vertical downward string is connected to the small ball at the lower position A; on the right there is a dashed circular arc indicating that the small ball moves from A along the circular arc to the upper-right position B; the angle \theta is marked between the dashed line pointing from O to B and the vertically downward OA direction; multiple horizontal arrows in the figure all point to the right and are labeled electric field E, indicating that the uniform electric field is horizontally to the right. Reasoning: Let the angle by which the small ball deviates from the vertically downward direction be \phi, point A is \phi=0, and point B is \phi=\theta=60^\circ. The speeds at points A and B are both 0, so applying conservation of energy from A to B: the work done by the electric field force qE\,L\sin\theta equals the increase in gravitational potential energy mgL(1-\cos\theta), that is, qEL\sin\theta=mgL(1-\cos\theta). Therefore E=\frac{mg(1-\cos\theta)}{q\sin\theta}. Substituting \theta=60^\circ, \cos60^\circ=\frac12, \sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}, gives E=\frac{mg(1/2)}{q(\sqrt3/2)}=\frac{mg}{\sqrt3 q}=\frac{\sqrt3 mg}{3q}. Along the circular arc, take the potential energy U(\phi)=mgL(1-\cos\phi)-qEL\sin\phi. The small ball is released from rest at A, and the total mechanical energy is taken as 0, so the kinetic energy K=-U(\phi). When the speed is maximum, the kinetic energy is maximum, that is, U(\phi) is minimum. Let \frac{dU}{d\phi}=mgL\sin\phi-qEL\cos\phi=0, obtaining \tan\phi=\frac{qE}{mg}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}, hence \phi=30^\circ. By conservation of energy, at \phi=30^\circ: \frac12 mv_{\max}^2=qEL\sin30^\circ-mgL(1-\cos30^\circ). Also qE=mg/\sqrt3, so \frac12 mv_{\max}^2=mgL\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}-1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=mgL\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-1\right). Therefore \frac{mv_{\max}^2}{L}=2mg\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-1\right). Write the equation in the radial direction pointing toward O: T-mg\cos\phi-qE\sin\phi=\frac{mv^2}{L}. Substituting \phi=30^\circ, qE=mg/\sqrt3 and the above expression: T=2mg\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-1\right)+mg\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{mg}{\sqrt3}\cdot\frac12 =2(\sqrt3-1)mg.

qEL\sin\theta=mgL(1-\cos\theta).
Therefore
E=\frac{mg(1-\cos\theta)}{q\sin\theta}.
Substituting \theta=60^\circ, \cos60^\circ=\frac12, \sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}, gives
E=\frac{mg(1/2)}{q(\sqrt3/2)}=\frac{mg}{\sqrt3 q}=\frac{\sqrt3 mg}{3q}.

Along the circular arc, take the potential energy
U(\phi)=mgL(1-\cos\phi)-qEL\sin\phi.
The small ball is released from rest at A, and the total mechanical energy is taken as 0, so the kinetic energy K=-U(\phi). When the speed is maximum, the kinetic energy is maximum, that is, U(\phi) is minimum. Let
\frac{dU}{d\phi}=mgL\sin\phi-qEL\cos\phi=0,
obtaining
\tan\phi=\frac{qE}{mg}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3},
hence \phi=30^\circ.

By conservation of energy, at \phi=30^\circ:
\frac12 mv_{\max}^2=qEL\sin30^\circ-mgL(1-\cos30^\circ).
Also qE=mg/\sqrt3, so
\frac12 mv_{\max}^2=mgL\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}-1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=mgL\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-1\right).
Therefore
\frac{mv_{\max}^2}{L}=2mg\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-1\right).

Write the equation in the radial direction pointing toward O:
T-mg\cos\phi-qE\sin\phi=\frac{mv^2}{L}.
Substituting \phi=30^\circ, qE=mg/\sqrt3 and the above expression:
T=2mg\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-1\right)+mg\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{mg}{\sqrt3}\cdot\frac12
=2(\sqrt3-1)mg.
